section_path: Abstract
Background and Objective
observations.text: Microbiota and their metabolites form a dynamic regulatory network that modulates the tumor microenvironment (TME) and immune cell functionality, emerging as critical targets in cancer immunotherapy. Despite remarkable advances in immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICIs), clinical efficacy remains limited by primary or acquired resistance in a substantial proportion of patients. Accumulating evidence indicates that the gut microbiota-metabolite-immune axis is a critical determinant of ICI responsiveness, but the underlying molecular mechanisms and tumor-specific regulatory patterns remain incompletely elucidated. This narrative review aims to systematically dissect the mechanistic interplay of this axis across diverse cancer types and synthesize current microbiota-targeted therapeutic strategies for improved immunotherapy outcomes.

section_path: Abstract
Methods
observations.text: We conducted a systematic literature search of PubMed for studies published between January 2019 and December 2025, with a particular focus on basic and translational research elucidating the roles of gut microbiota and their metabolites in cancer immunotherapy across various malignancies.

section_path: Abstract
Key Content and Findings
observations.text: This review elucidates the molecular mechanisms by which core metabolites regulate antitumor immunity, synthesizes characteristic microbial signatures across gastrointestinal and non-gastrointestinal cancers. Furthermore, we evaluate the translational potential of intervention strategies, including fecal microbiota transplantation, probiotic supplementation, and engineered microbes, as adjuvants to enhance ICI efficacy and overcome resistance.

section_path: Abstract
Conclusions
observations.text: Microbiota-based personalized therapeutic strategies are increasingly recognized as promising tools to modulate antitumor immunity and improve immunotherapy outcomes. Systematic profiling of the gut microbiota-metabolite-immune axis across cancer types will facilitate the development of precision interventions to overcome ICI resistance. Future research integrating multi-omics approaches and large-scale clinical trials is pivotal to translate mechanistic insights into clinically viable therapies, ultimately revolutionizing the landscape of cancer immuno-oncology.

section_path: Introduction
observations.text: The human body hosts a vast and complex microbial ecosystem, comprising approximately 40 trillion microorganisms comprising around 3,000 distinct microbial species (1). The human gastrointestinal microbial community represents a highly intricate ecosystem, with the colon serving as the primary habitat for bacterial colonization and playing a decisive role in shaping the total bacterial load within the human body (2). These microbial communities exhibit interindividual variability and critically maintain systemic homeostasis, immunity, metabolism, and cancer pathogenesis (3,4).

section_path: Introduction
observations.text: A growing body of research has elucidated that gut microbiota plays a crucial role in the therapeutic efficacy of immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICIs) (5-9). In recent years, immunotherapy has emerged as a prominent therapeutic approach in the management of malignant tumors. The earliest identified ICIs primarily consisted of three categories: anti-programmed cell death protein 1 (PD-1), anti-programmed death-ligand 1 (PD-L1), and anti-cytotoxic T-lymphocyte-associated antigen-4 (CTLA-4) monoclonal antibodies. Recent discoveries of novel immune checkpoints have not only expanded the repertoire of therapeutic targets but also provided new perspectives for personalized cancer treatment. Noteworthy examples are lymphocyte-activation gene-3 (LAG-3), T-cell immunoglobulin and mucin-domain-containing 3 (TIM-3), T-cell immunoglobulin and ITIM domain (TIGIT), and V-domain Ig suppressor of T-cell activation (VISTA), among others (10).

section_path: Introduction
observations.text: However, a notable proportion of patients who initially respond to ICI therapy ultimately develop acquired resistance (11), representing a major clinical challenge. Therefore, current advancements in gastrointestinal microbiome research represent a meaningful and novel direction for addressing immunotherapy resistance in oncology. However, the underlying molecular mechanisms through which gut microbiota and their metabolites influence immunotherapy efficacy remain poorly understood across cancer types. This review systematically examines microbiota-metabolite interactions affecting ICI outcomes and explores therapeutic implications. We present this article in accordance with the Narrative Review reporting checklist (available at https://tcr.amegroups.com/article/view/10.21037/tcr-2025-1992/rc).

The eligible references included peer-reviewed, English-language articles published between January 1, 2019 and December 30, 2025, and contained the following MeSH terms: “Carcinomas, Esophageal Neoplasms, Gastric Cancer, Pancreas Cancers, Colorectal Cancer, Hepatocellular Carcinomas, Lung Cancer, melanoma, Renal Cancer, Microbiotas, Microbiome, Immune Checkpoint Blockers, Immune Checkpoint Inhibitor, Fecal Microbiota Transplantations, Probiotics”; and free text: “PD-1, PD-L1, short-chain fatty acids, bile acids, tryptophan metabolites, inosine, engineered microbes”. section_path: Reciprocal regulation within the gut microbiota-metabolite-immune axis
observations.text: The core of the gut microbiota-metabolite-immune axis lies in the production of diverse bioactive metabolites by the gut microbiota through its metabolic activities. These metabolites act as molecular messengers within the axis, not only regulating host energy metabolism and nutrient absorption but, more crucially, reprogramming antitumor immune responses (11). Notably, the dynamic nature of this axis is reflected in the ability of these metabolites to translocate from the intestinal lumen into systemic circulation, exerting pleiotropic effects on both local and systemic antitumor immunity, thereby modulating therapeutic responses to ICIs across multiple cancer types (6,12,13). Figure 1 and Table 2 systematically illustrate the key node networks of metabolite-immune interactions within this axis, revealing its translational potential as a druggable target.

section_path: Reciprocal regulation within the gut microbiota-metabolite-immune axis
observations.text: The integrated mechanisms by which gut microbial metabolites shape antitumor immunity by steering the fate of immune cells. Butyrate, the best-studied SCFA, exerts multifaceted and context-dependent effects: it inhibits HDAC activity to activate M2-like tumor-associated macrophages in lung cancer, yet concurrently enhances the cytotoxic capacity of CD8^{+} T cells, boosts ROS production, and thereby suppresses tumor-cell proliferation and metastasis. Tryptophan catabolites activate the AhR via the IDO1-Kyn axis, expanding Tregs and fostering an immunosuppressive niche. Among secondary BAs, UDCA degrades TGF-β and consequently restrains Treg differentiation, whereas isoDCA impairs dendritic-cell function and indirectly promotes Treg accumulation. Inosine engages the A2AR to raise intracellular cAMP, tipping the balance toward Th1-cell differentiation. The net outcome of these opposing metabolic signals determines whether the tumor micro-environment remains cold or becomes hot. Collectively, the scheme underscores that the tripartite interplay among microbial metabolites, host receptors, and immune cells constitutes a central rheostat of cancer immunosurveillance. section_path: Reciprocal regulation within the gut microbiota-metabolite-immune axis
Gut microbiota-metabolite-mediated immune reprogramming
observations.text: The gut microbiota, as a highly complex ecosystem, produces a diverse array of bioactive metabolites through metabolic activities, which serve as the initial signals of the gut microbiota-metabolite-immune axis. Functioning as the key signaling branch of this axis, these metabolites systematically regulate both innate and adaptive immunity through mechanisms such as receptor engagement, epigenetic remodeling, and metabolic reprogramming. This dynamic regulatory network demonstrates that distinct microbial communities can exert differential effects on the immune system via their specific metabolic products. The following sections will focus on various core metabolites, elaborating on their source microorganisms, characteristic functions, and the immune regulatory mechanisms they mediate.

section_path: Reciprocal regulation within the gut microbiota-metabolite-immune axis
Gut microbiota-metabolite-mediated immune reprogramming
Short-chain fatty acids (SCFAs): epigenetic and metabolic regulators of antitumor immunity
observations.text: SCFAs are produced as metabolic by-products during the fermentation of complex carbohydrates and dietary fiber. This bioconversion is predominantly driven by bacterial species within the Bacteroidetes phylum, particularly those belonging to the genera Bacteroides, Prevotella, Parabacteroides, and Alistipes. Their high expression of carbohydrate-active enzymes confers a robust degradative capacity, enabling efficient substrate utilization (26-28).

section_path: Reciprocal regulation within the gut microbiota-metabolite-immune axis
Gut microbiota-metabolite-mediated immune reprogramming
Short-chain fatty acids (SCFAs): epigenetic and metabolic regulators of antitumor immunity
observations.text: Butyrate exhibits antitumor properties through multiple, context-dependent pathways. A key mechanism involves histone deacetylase (HDAC) inhibition. It suppresses HDAC activity, butyrate increases protein acetylation, thereby downregulating NFATc3 and inhibiting tumor cell proliferation (29) yet paradoxically promotes lung cancer metastasis by suppressing HDAC2, drives M2 macrophage polarization and upregulates H19 expression in tumor cells (30). Faecalibaculum rodentium-derived metabolites propionate and butyrate enhance histone acetylation to promote progenitor-exhausted CD8^{+} T cells expansion, thereby activating antitumor immune responses (31).

section_path: Reciprocal regulation within the gut microbiota-metabolite-immune axis
Gut microbiota-metabolite-mediated immune reprogramming
Short-chain fatty acids (SCFAs): epigenetic and metabolic regulators of antitumor immunity
observations.text: G-protein-coupled receptor 109A (GPR109A) and reactive oxygen species (ROS) may represent critical pathways through which butyrate regulates tumor proliferation and therapeutic efficacy. Beyond epigenetic modulation, butyrate enhances CD8^{+} T cell cytotoxicity via the GPR109A/HOPX signaling axis, offering therapeutic potential in gastric cancer (GC) (14), and induces apoptosis in colonic epithelial cells through GPR109A binding (32). In hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC), butyrate supplementation activates calcium signaling and ROS generation, disrupting intracellular calcium homeostasis and attenuating tumor growth and metastasis (33). Additionally, butyrate modulates miR-22 expression in hepatocytes, promoting apoptosis via ROS accumulation, cytochrome C release, and caspase-3 activation (34).

Short-chain fatty acids (SCFAs): epigenetic and metabolic regulators of antitumor immunity
observations.text: Subsequent mechanistic studies have delineated that butyrate enhances anti-PD-1 efficacy by activating CD8^{+} T cells through multiple, complementary routes. It intensifies T-cell receptor (TCR) signaling (15) and engages Toll-like receptor 5 (TLR5), triggering NF-κB-dependent transcriptional programs (6) that expand and energize the cytotoxic T-cell pool (35,36). These findings highlight the considerable potential of butyrate to serve as a therapeutic biomarker that modulates CD8^{+} T-cell-mediated antitumor immunity.

section_path: Reciprocal regulation within the gut microbiota-metabolite-immune axis
Gut microbiota-metabolite-mediated immune reprogramming
Short-chain fatty acids (SCFAs): epigenetic and metabolic regulators of antitumor immunity
observations.text: Butyrate exerts bidirectional, context-dependent immunomodulatory effects by remodeling dendritic cell (DC) function. Its core mechanism involves inhibiting DC maturation markers—blocking CD80/CD86 upregulation and preventing pro-T helper 17 (Th17) polarization—to differentially regulate T cell responses. In anti-CTLA-4 therapy, this reduces DC-mediated T cell activation, impairing intratumoral infiltration of inducible T-cell co-stimulator (ICOS)^{+} tumor-specific T cells and memory T cells, thus weakening efficacy (16). Conversely, in myeloma, butyrate-producing Prevotella melaninogenica suppresses the DC-Th17 axis to reduce Th17 accumulation, promotes effector CD8^{+} T cell differentiation, and synergizes with anti-PD-L1 for antitumor effects (37). The paradoxical observations outlined above reveal that SCFA-mediated immune regulation is profoundly context-dependent, with functional outcomes dictated by tumor-specific immune infiltration landscapes and host metabolic states. This mechanistic complexity necessitates that future studies transcend reductive dichotomies, instead establishing predictive models grounded in integrated multi-omics analyses.

section_path: Reciprocal regulation within the gut microbiota-metabolite-immune axis
Gut microbiota-metabolite-mediated immune reprogramming
Short-chain fatty acids (SCFAs): epigenetic and metabolic regulators of antitumor immunity
observations.text: Propionate and valerate also contribute to tumor immunotherapy. Notably, propionate produced by Akkermansia muciniphila (Akk) induces tumor cell apoptosis through mechanisms involving mitochondrial dysfunction and caspase activation (38). Both valerate and butyrate modulate mechanistic target of rapamycin (mTOR) signaling, a central regulator of cellular metabolism, while concurrently inhibiting class I HDAC activity. This dual mechanism facilitates metabolic and epigenetic reprogramming, resulting in upregulated expression of effector molecules such as CD25, interferon-γ (IFN-γ), and tumor necrosis factor-alpha (TNF-α). Consequently, these changes enhance the antitumor activity of antigen-specific cytotoxic T lymphocytes (CTLs) and chimeric antigen receptor (CAR) T cells, as demonstrated in preclinical melanoma and pancreatic cancer models (17).

section_path: Reciprocal regulation within the gut microbiota-metabolite-immune axis
Gut microbiota-metabolite-mediated immune reprogramming
Tryptophan metabolism: a key node in gut microbiota-immune crosstalk
observations.text: Gut microbiota metabolizes dietary tryptophan into bioactive compounds via distinct enzymatic systems in species such as Bacteroides ovatus, Clostridium limosum, Enterococcus faecalis, Escherichia coli, and Clostridium sporogenes (39). These metabolites, including indole, indole-3-lactic acid (ILA), indole-3-acrylic acid (IAcrA), indole-3-propionic acid (IPA), indole-3-acetic acid (IAA), indole-3-aldehyde (I3A), and tryptamine, play pivotal roles in regulating barrier function, immunity, inflammation, and metabolism (40).

section_path: Reciprocal regulation within the gut microbiota-metabolite-immune axis
Gut microbiota-metabolite-mediated immune reprogramming
Tryptophan metabolism: a key node in gut microbiota-immune crosstalk
observations.text: Aryl hydrocarbon receptor (AhR) mediates tryptophan metabolite effects on immune signaling and homeostasis (41,42). Kynurenine (Kyn) exerts its immunosuppressive function by activating AhR, which promotes regulatory T cell (Treg) differentiation (19). I3A has been demonstrated to activates AhR to strengthen barrier integrity (43), induce cAMP response element-binding protein (CREB) phosphorylation for CD8^{+} T cell proliferation and maturation (13) and engage the AhR/interleukin-22 (IL-22) axis to protect intestinal barrier integrity, modulate gut microbial composition and function, and enhance immunotherapeutic efficacy (44).

section_path: Reciprocal regulation within the gut microbiota-metabolite-immune axis
Gut microbiota-metabolite-mediated immune reprogramming
Tryptophan metabolism: a key node in gut microbiota-immune crosstalk
observations.text: Among these tryptophan metabolites, Kyn has immunosuppressive effects. Elevated serum Kyn to tryptophan ratios correlate with suppressed T-cell proliferation and poorer clinical outcomes in melanoma and renal cell carcinoma (RCC) (18). Reducing this ratio can inhibit Treg activity while enhancing effector T-cell function, thereby augmenting anti-PD-1 efficacy (20). Similarly, Indole-3-carboxaldehyde (ICA) from Lactobacillus gallinarum can inhibit enzyme IDO1, decreasing Kyn production, impairing Treg differentiation (21).

observations.text: Together, these findings underscore the need to investigate tryptophan metabolites to elucidate mechanisms underlying ICI therapy. Notably, I3A-mediated activation of this signaling cascade mitigates ICI-induced colitis, offering a promising strategy to manage treatment-related adverse effects (45). These insights open novel avenues for optimizing therapeutic efficacy while minimizing complications, firmly establishing tryptophan metabolism as a central node in the gut microbiota-metabolite-immune axis.

Bile acids (BAs): microbial modulators of antitumor immunity
observations.text: BAs are formed through host-microbe co-metabolism. Primary BAs synthesized by hepatocytes are enzymatically remodeled by gut bacteria through deconjugation, dehydroxylation, and other transformations, generating secondary BAs and other metabolites (46).

section_path: Reciprocal regulation within the gut microbiota-metabolite-immune axis
Gut microbiota-metabolite-mediated immune reprogramming
Bile acids (BAs): microbial modulators of antitumor immunity
observations.text: Emerging research has cast light on the complex crosstalk between microbial-derived BAs and antitumor immunity, revealing starkly opposing effects on CD8^{+} T cell fate. Deoxycholic acid (DCA), a secondary BA generated through microbial metabolism, suppresses CD8^{+} T cell effector functions and promotes tumor progression in murine models (47), whereas 3-oxo-Δ4,6-lithocholic acid blocks CD8^{+} T cell-intrinsic androgen receptor signaling, redirecting their differentiation toward stem-like memory T cells (48). Separately, isodeoxycholic acid (isoDCA), another secondary BA, modulates DC activity, upregulating Foxp3 expression, and expanding Treg populations (22).

section_path: Reciprocal regulation within the gut microbiota-metabolite-immune axis
Gut microbiota-metabolite-mediated immune reprogramming
Bile acids (BAs): microbial modulators of antitumor immunity
observations.text: Ursodeoxycholic acid (UDCA) plays a pivotal role in maintaining intestinal barrier integrity. Interestingly, UDCA exhibits context-dependent dual functionality, displaying either pro-apoptotic or anti-apoptotic effects depending on cellular and environmental conditions (23). In tumor-bearing mice, UDCA inhibits Treg differentiation and activation by degrading transforming growth factor-β (TGF-β), thereby potentiating antitumor immune responses (49).

section_path: Reciprocal regulation within the gut microbiota-metabolite-immune axis
Gut microbiota-metabolite-mediated immune reprogramming
Bile acids (BAs): microbial modulators of antitumor immunity
observations.text: Although the role of BAs in ICI therapy remains underexplored, their mechanisms in modulating tumor progression have garnered considerable scientific interest (50,51). Given the current depth of understanding regarding bile acid-tumor-immune interactions, continued investigation into their roles within the context of ICI therapy holds significant promise for advancing therapeutic strategies and achieving novel breakthroughs in cancer immunotherapy, further solidifying BAs as key mediators of the gut microbiota-metabolite-immune axis.

section_path: Reciprocal regulation within the gut microbiota-metabolite-immune axis
Gut microbiota-metabolite-mediated immune reprogramming
Inosine: a purine metabolite at the metabolic-immune interface
observations.text: Inosine is a critical intermediary in the purine nucleotide metabolic pathway and is synthesized by gut microbiota such as Bifidobacterium pseudolongum, Lactobacillus johnsonii, and bacteria of the genus Olsenella (24). This microbial-derived metabolite plays essential roles in post-transcriptional gene regulation, modulation of metabolic enzyme activities, and integration into cellular signaling networks (25). Notably, immune checkpoint blockade (ICB) therapy impairs gut barrier integrity, facilitating the translocation of inosine into the systemic circulation and subsequent activation of antitumor T cells, establishing inosine as the key molecule mediating the enhancement of ICB efficacy by these bacteria (24).

section_path: Reciprocal regulation within the gut microbiota-metabolite-immune axis
Gut microbiota-metabolite-mediated immune reprogramming
Inosine: a purine metabolite at the metabolic-immune interface
observations.text: Currently, inosine exerts three principal effects in antitumor therapy. Firstly, it markedly enhances tumor immunogenicity. Zhang et al. employed advanced metabolomic profiling to analyze plasma samples from melanoma-bearing mice undergoing ICI treatment, revealing a novel mechanism: inosine specifically inhibits ubiquitin-like modifier-activating enzyme 6 (UBA6) activity within tumor cells, leading to a marked increase in tumor immunogenicity (52). This dual-purpose finding identifies UBA6 as a therapeutic target and rationalizes inosine-based combination therapy.

section_path: Reciprocal regulation within the gut microbiota-metabolite-immune axis
Gut microbiota-metabolite-mediated immune reprogramming
Inosine: a purine metabolite at the metabolic-immune interface
observations.text: Secondly, inosine plays distinct roles in immune cell modulation and metabolic support. Microbial-derived inosine binds to adenosine A2A receptors on T lymphocytes, triggering activation of the cAMP-CREB signaling cascade. This pathway facilitates the differentiation and tumor infiltration of T helper 1 (Th1) cells within the tumor microenvironment (TME), amplifying antitumor immune responses (24).

section_path: Reciprocal regulation within the gut microbiota-metabolite-immune axis
Gut microbiota-metabolite-mediated immune reprogramming
Inosine: a purine metabolite at the metabolic-immune interface
observations.text: Thirdly, and most critically, inosine functions as a compensatory metabolic substrate that sustains T cell bioenergetics under glucose-restricted TME conditions. Wang et al. experimentally demonstrated that effector T cells utilize inosine as an alternative energy source during glucose deprivation, sustaining their survival, proliferation, and cytotoxic functions (53). Clinically, this dual functionality holds therapeutic promise. In solid tumors exhibiting inosine metabolic deficiencies, exogenous inosine supplementation may restore immune cell metabolic fitness. Such interventions could potentiate the efficacy of ICIs and adoptive T cell therapies by overcoming tumor-imposed metabolic constraints.

section_path: Reciprocal regulation within the gut microbiota-metabolite-immune axis
Gut microbiota-metabolite-mediated immune reprogramming
Inosine: a purine metabolite at the metabolic-immune interface
observations.text: Inosine also has been demonstrated to have significant translational potential in CAR-T therapy, representing a cutting-edge advancement in adoptive cell immunotherapy (54,55). As a critical microbial metabolite in cancer immunotherapy, inosine exerts multifaceted biological effects through its ability to regulate immune cell functionality, optimize metabolic pathways, and remodel the TME. These mechanisms collectively enhance antitumor immunity by promoting T cell activation and survival under metabolically challenging conditions while simultaneously improving tumor immunogenicity. By integrating inosine supplementation with existing immunotherapies, such as ICIs and CAR-T, researchers may overcome current limitations in treatment efficacy, particularly for tumors resistant to conventional approaches.

section_path: Reciprocal regulation within the gut microbiota-metabolite-immune axis
Immune feedback on microbial communities
observations.text: The bidirectionality of the axis is evidenced by clinical observations: antibiotic use perturbs microbiota diversity and BA metabolism, diminishing SCFA pools and abrogating ICI efficacy in RCC, melanoma and non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) patients (56,57). Conversely, ICI responders exhibit restored microbial α-diversity with enrichment of Akk and Ruminococcaceae (58,59), suggesting that effective antitumor immunity reciprocally selects for beneficial taxa. However, the molecular effectors mediating this feedback remain largely uncharacterized in solid tumors, representing a critical knowledge gap. This loop underscores that the axis is not unidirectional but a dynamic, self-modulating network wherein perturbation at any node propagates systemically.

section_path: Microbiome-immune axis in cancer immunotherapy: diverse mechanistic pathways across tumor types
observations.text: Building on these mechanistic insights into the microbiota-metabolite-immune axis, we next examine how these principles manifest across diverse malignancies, where tumor-specific microenvironments critically modulate therapeutic outcomes (5-7). This recognition has intensified the need to elucidate the mechanistic pathways through which specific microbial taxa and their metabolic byproducts influence ICI activity. The microbiota exerts dual immunomodulatory effects, regulating both innate and adaptive immune responses within the TME while simultaneously shaping systemic antitumor immunity (60,61). These tumor-type-specific interactions manifest through distinct mechanisms across malignancies, as detailed below (Figure 2).

section_path: Microbiome-immune axis in cancer immunotherapy: diverse mechanistic pathways across tumor types
Esophageal carcinoma
observations.text: The therapeutic efficacy of immunotherapy is intrinsically linked to the tumor immune microenvironment (TIME), wherein intratumoral microbial communities emerge as critical modulators. These microbial populations influence patient responses to ICIs through dynamic remodeling of the TIME. Streptococcus enrichment in responders correlates with enhanced CD8^{+} T-cell infiltration (62) while Fusobacterium nucleatum (Fn) drives resistance through PD-L1 upregulation and T cell suppression (63,64). Dual immunosuppressive pathways significantly impair local antitumor immunity, resulting in markedly reduced ICI responsiveness among patients with esophageal squamous cell carcinoma (ESCC) (64). Moreover, a prospective study has simultaneously revealed that low gut α-diversity also predicts poor response and shorter survival in the same cancer type (65). Consequently, the ESCC microenvironment should be viewed as an integrated ecosystem in which the collective action of the entire gut microbial community, rather than a single pathobiont, dictates therapeutic outcomes. Liang’s team systematically analyzed the gut microbial composition of 68 patients with ESCC and established a predictive model with high accuracy of neoadjuvant immunochemotherapy (NICT) response in ESCC using machine learning-based baseline gut bacterial strain signatures (66). Enabling precision medicine approaches for patient stratification and therapeutic target identification holds significant promise for future clinical translation.

section_path: Microbiome-immune axis in cancer immunotherapy: diverse mechanistic pathways across tumor types
GC
observations.text: GC arises from multifactorial etiopathogenesis, with intratumoral microbial communities emerging as critical modulators of disease progression. Among these, Helicobacter pylori (H. pylori) occupies a central role in gastric carcinogenesis, employing both direct virulence factor-mediated mechanisms and indirect microbiome-modulating strategies (67). H. pylori effectively subverts antitumor immunity by creating an immune-protective niche for malignant cells while upregulating PD-L1 expression in gastric epithelium—a key immune evasion mechanism that inhibits cytotoxic T-cell-mediated tumor clearance (68).

section_path: Microbiome-immune axis in cancer immunotherapy: diverse mechanistic pathways across tumor types
GC
observations.text: While H. pylori continues to dominate diagnostic and therapeutic pipelines, large-scale microbiome surveys of GC patients from two demographically distinct cohorts now reveal significant enrichments of Lactobacillus, Streptococcus, Prevotella and Bacteroides within tumor tissue (69). These data underscore that the GC microbiome extends well beyond H. pylori, warranting comprehensive investigation of multi-species microbial networks that collectively influence disease progression and therapeutic response. H. pylori upregulates PD-L1 to subvert immunity, but a study also found that Lactobacillus abundance correlates with enhanced microbial α-diversity, superior anti-PD-1/PD-L1 response rates and a favorable progression-free survival trend (70). These convergent findings identify H. pylori and Lactobacillus as a keystone taxon whose enrichment predicts enhanced ICI responsiveness while preserving microbiome homeostasis.

section_path: Microbiome-immune axis in cancer immunotherapy: diverse mechanistic pathways across tumor types
Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC)
observations.text: PDAC is the most common malignant pancreatic tumor and the third leading cause of cancer-related death worldwide. Currently, the standard treatment for PDAC is surgical resection followed by adjuvant chemotherapy (71). Interestingly, preclinical studies have shown that orthotopic PDAC models are intrinsically resistant to anti-PD-1 monotherapy, but they can become sensitive to treatment after the microbiota is depleted by oral antibiotics. Studies have indicated that three bacterial species, namely Elizabethkingia, Enterobacteriaceae, and Mycoplasmataceae play a role in influencing both the progression of PDAC and the response to PD-1 treatment (72). This phenotypic shift correlates mechanistically with enhanced CD4^{+} and CD8^{+} T-cell activation within the TME.

section_path: Microbiome-immune axis in cancer immunotherapy: diverse mechanistic pathways across tumor types
Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC)
observations.text: This was corroborated by a FMT study in which microbiota from long-term PDAC survivors triggered robust CD8^{+} T-cell activation while curbing Foxp3^{+} Tregs, an effect traced to Pseudoxanthomonas, Streptomyces, Saccharopolyspora and Bacillus clausii (73). Adding a metabolic layer, the microbial-derived metabolite trimethylamine N-oxide (TMAO) has been shown to amplify antitumor immunity against PDAC (74). Viewing the TME as an integrated ecosystem, Li et al. further employed spatial profiling in murine models to map the co-localization and dynamic interplay between microbes and immune cells, offering a roadmap for future mechanistic dissection (75).

section_path: Microbiome-immune axis in cancer immunotherapy: diverse mechanistic pathways across tumor types
HCC
observations.text: HCC is a highly aggressive malignancy with dismal prognostic outcomes. It ranks among the leading causes of global cancer-related mortality, thereby imposing a substantial burden on public health (76). Recent clinical trials have shown that ICIs targeting PD-1 have demonstrated promising efficacy in the treatment of HCC (77,78). Building on these therapeutic advancements, emerging research has elucidated the crucial associations between the composition of the gut microbiota and the clinical efficacy of PD-1 immunotherapy in hepatobiliary malignancies. Mechanistic investigations have identified Akk and specific Ruminococcaceae species as microbial signatures correlated with enhanced therapeutic responses (12). Moreover, multi-center prospective cohorts, leveraging paired fecal metagenomics and metabolomics, have convergently identified a cluster of HCC-immunotherapy-favorable taxa—Lachnospiraceae-GAM79, Alistipes sp. Marseille-P5997, Ruminococcus, Erysipelotrichaceae-GAM147 (79), Lachnoclostridium and Lachnospiraceae (80)—enriched in responders, whereas Veillonellaceae (79) and Prevotella 9 (80) dominate in progressors. Parallel metabolic profiling of these signatures has mapped their functional output, laying a solid foundation for mechanistic dissection and therapeutic exploitation. Isobutyric acid produced by gut Bifidobacterium enhances anti-PD-1 immunotherapy efficacy in HCC by activating CD8^{+} T cells to secrete IFN-γ, thereby inhibiting the JAK1/STAT3 pathway (81).

section_path: Microbiome-immune axis in cancer immunotherapy: diverse mechanistic pathways across tumor types
HCC
observations.text: A prospective cohort study involving 80 HCC patients undergoing ICI therapy further validates these findings. Through an integrated analysis of gut microbial composition, α-diversity metrics, and metabolomic profiles, researchers have identified predictive bacterial signatures for ICI responsiveness, notably Actinomyces sp. strain ICM47 and Anaerotruncus senegalensis, while elucidating the prognostic significance of microbially-derived metabolites such as secondary bile acids and SCFAs (82). Collectively, these discoveries provide mechanistic insights into microbiota-mediated immunomodulation in HCC and establish a robust foundation for microbiome-based precision oncology strategies.

section_path: Microbiome-immune axis in cancer immunotherapy: diverse mechanistic pathways across tumor types
Colorectal cancer (CRC)
observations.text: ICIs exhibit limited efficacy in CRC, except in patients with mismatch repair deficiency (dMMR) or high microsatellite instability (MSI-H) (83,84). Emerging evidence reveals that gut microbiota modulates CRC antitumor immunity through multifaceted mechanisms. Studies demonstrated that Lactobacillus rhamnosus GG (LGG) (8) and Fn (85) both upregulates activates the cGAS/STING axis to enhance anti-tumor immunity. LGG activates the cGAS/STING axis in CRC and melanoma models, which in turn stimulates type I interferon production in DCs (8). Fn activates NF-κB (p65) and induces PD-L1 expression while promoting IFN-γ^{+} CD8^{+} tumor-infiltrating lymphocyte (TIL) accumulation, thereby potentiating PD-1/PD-L1 blockade efficacy (85). More recently, mechanistic insights have expanded further. Fn-derived butyrate was shown to inhibit HDAC3/8 activity, suppressing PD-1 in CD8^{+} TILs, enhancing tumor cell clearance (9).

section_path: Microbiome-immune axis in cancer immunotherapy: diverse mechanistic pathways across tumor types
Colorectal cancer (CRC)
observations.text: Concurrently, Kang et al. identified Roseburia intestinalis as a butyrate-producing commensal bacterium that plays a significant role in suppressing CRC progression and enhancing sensitivity to anti-PD-1 therapy through CD8^{+} T cell-dependent mechanisms (6). Furthermore, Lactobacillus gallinarum was discovered to synthesize ICA, a dual-function metabolite that inhibits tumor IDO1 expression and Kyn biosynthesis, while also competitively antagonizing Kyn-mediated AhR activation. This dual action of ICA suppresses Treg differentiation and enhances CD8^{+} T cell cytotoxicity, ultimately improving PD-1 therapeutic responses (21). These data support the potential of microbial metabolites as ICI adjuvants, offering new avenues for optimizing cancer immunotherapy strategies.

section_path: Microbiome-immune axis in cancer immunotherapy: diverse mechanistic pathways across tumor types
Colorectal cancer (CRC)
observations.text: Microbial factors suppress CD8^{+} T cells via myeloid-derived suppressor cells (MDSCs), abrogating PD-1 therapy efficacy and promoting tumor progression. Liu et al. revealed that Peptostreptococcus anaerobius infection promotes MDSC accumulation and activation, creating an immunosuppressive microenvironment that abrogates PD-1 responsiveness through CD8^{+} T cell inhibition (7). Similarly, the microbial metabolite 4-hydroxyphenylacetic acid can promote the infiltration of polymorphonuclear myeloid-derived suppressor cells (PMN-MDSCs) into the TME, thereby suppressing CD8^{+} T cell-mediated anti-tumor responses and facilitating CRC progression in vivo (86).

section_path: Microbiome-immune axis in cancer immunotherapy: diverse mechanistic pathways across tumor types
Non-gastrointestinal tumors
observations.text: Current research has revealed that microbiota can infiltrate tumor tissues through three primary pathways to influence tumor progression and therapeutic outcomes: direct mucosal invasion, penetration into adjacent normal tissues (NAT), and systemic dissemination via the circulatory system (87). This phenomenon extends beyond gastrointestinal malignancies, indicating that gut microbiota significantly contributes to the pathogenesis of non-digestive tract tumors. In 2015, two landmark studies published in Science, first elucidated the mechanistic role of gut microbiota in modulating immunotherapy responses in melanoma, establishing a critical foundation for this field. These two studies first elucidated the underlying mechanisms by which Commensal Bifidobacterium, B. thetaiotaomicron, and B. fragilis in the gut microbiota mediate the responses to melanoma immunotherapy (5,88). Subsequent investigations have systematically compared responders and non-responders to immunotherapy through comprehensive analyses of gut microbiome diversity and compositional variations, complemented by animal experimentation. These studies consistently demonstrate that patients with favorable gut microbial profiles exhibit enhanced systemic immunity and anti-tumor responses. Notably, FMT experiments have confirmed that germ-free mice receiving transplants from responder patients acquire improved immunocompetence and tumor control capabilities (89-91).

section_path: Microbiome-immune axis in cancer immunotherapy: diverse mechanistic pathways across tumor types
Non-gastrointestinal tumors
observations.text: Matson et al. demonstrated that elevated abundances of Bifidobacterium longum, Collinsella aerofaciens, and Enterococcus faecium in responders correlate with improved tumor control, enhanced T-cell responses, and increased efficacy of anti-PD-L1 therapy (91). Parallel research by Gopalakrishnan et al. identified Ruminococcaceae and Faecalibacterium as beneficial taxa that amplify antigen presentation-mediated systemic anti-tumor immunity while enhancing effector T-cell functionality in both peripheral circulation and TME (89). Macandog et al. discovered that MHC class I-restricted peptides derived from flagellin-associated genes in Lachnospiraceae (FLach) exhibit structural homology with tumor-associated antigens. Their work demonstrated that detection of FLach-reactive CD8^{+} T cells in complete responders prior to ICI treatment, coupled with FLach peptide administration, significantly enhances anti-tumor immunity (90). Recent investigations have revealed that Lactobacillus reuteri promotes I3A production (13) and exercise-induced microbiota-derived formate (92) synergistically enhance CD8^{+} T-cell proliferation and induces IFN-γ and granzyme B (GzmB) secretion in melanoma models, thereby potentiating tumor cell cytotoxicity.

section_path: Microbiome-immune axis in cancer immunotherapy: diverse mechanistic pathways across tumor types
Non-gastrointestinal tumors
observations.text: Similarly, accumulating evidence since 2018 has consistently demonstrated that oral antibiotic use diminishes the clinical efficacy of immunotherapy in patients with advanced or metastatic RCC (56,57,93). These findings are corroborated by preclinical studies utilizing fecal microbiota transplantation (FMT) models, which further validate the positive correlation between microbial diversity and clinical benefits from ICI therapy (58,59). Derosa et al. identified several bacterial taxa associated with favorable prognosis, including Eubacterium rectale, Eubacterium siraeum, Dorea longicatena, Akk, Alistipes senegalensis and Bacteroides salyersiae (58). Consistently, Salgia et al. revealed increased relative abundance of Akk in patients deriving clinical benefits from ICIs, reinforcing its role as a keystone species in therapeutic responsiveness (59).

section_path: Microbiome-immune axis in cancer immunotherapy: diverse mechanistic pathways across tumor types
Non-gastrointestinal tumors
observations.text: Although cohort studies and high-throughput sequencing have identified multiple bacteria associated with ICI efficacy, their causal mechanisms remain unproven. The TME is a complex, dynamic ecosystem; attributing efficacy differences to a handful of species is an oversimplification. Future studies should integrate spatial transcriptomics, in situ imaging, and microbial tracing to generate three-dimensional maps of bacteria-immune-tumor interactions, opening avenues for optimizing microbiota-based immunotherapy.

section_path: Immunotherapeutic strategies targeting the gut microbiota
observations.text: Given that tumor-type-specific microbial signatures shape ICI responsiveness as reviewed above, developing targeted microbiota-directed interventions emerges as a logical therapeutic frontier. These mechanistic insights establish microbiota-directed interventions as a promising frontier in oncology therapeutic development, particularly for enhancing ICI efficacy through targeted microbial modulation (Figure 3).

section_path: Immunotherapeutic strategies targeting the gut microbiota
FMT
observations.text: FMT is a therapeutic intervention involving the transfer of donor gut microbiota, which has been established as a primary strategy for whole-microbiome reconstitution and is formally recommended in clinical guidelines for recurrent Clostridioides difficile infection (rCDI). FMT has emerged as a promising therapeutic modality for diverse conditions, including inflammatory bowel disease (IBD), metabolic syndrome, and solid malignancies. Despite decades of clinical reliance on combined chemotherapy and immunotherapy regimens, the limited efficacy of ICIs as monotherapy has driven exploration of microbiome-based therapeutic adjuvants. Seminal work in 2018 demonstrated that transferring fecal microbiota from ICI-responsive patients into germ-free or antibiotic-pretreated murine models enhanced ICI antitumor efficacy, establishing a causal link between gut microbiota composition and therapeutic outcomes (94). Subsequent studies have further validated this approach. Derosa et al. observed that fecal transplants from ICI-refractory RCC patients conferred reduced treatment responsiveness in RCC-bearing mice, while Wang et al. reported that transferring microbiota from microsatellite-stable colorectal cancer (MSS-CRC) patients with high Fn burdens into germ-free MSS-CRC models increased sensitivity to anti-PD-1 therapy (9).

section_path: Immunotherapeutic strategies targeting the gut microbiota
FMT
observations.text: Clinical studies confirm FMT’s potential to enhance ICI efficacy. Baruch et al. reported two partial and one complete response in refractory melanoma patients receiving FMT plus anti-PD-1, demonstrating the feasibility of FMT as an adjunct to immunotherapy (95). Building on these findings, Routy et al. performed a multicenter phase I trial in 20 treatment-naïve patients with advanced melanoma, combining healthy donor FMT with PD-1 inhibitors (nivolumab or pembrolizumab). The trial reported an objective response rate of 65%, including four complete responses, while concurrently establishing the safety profile of FMT in this therapeutic context (96). Recent metagenomic analyses further identified favorable mycobiome enterotypes that enrich butyrate-producing bacteria and enhance CD8^{+} T cell infiltration when selected as donors (36). Based on this study, clinicians could optimize therapeutic precision. This multi-kingdom approach represents a paradigm shift from traditional bacteria-centric donor screening, potentially improving patient outcomes in cancer immunotherapy. Prospective validation across diverse malignancies will be essential to establish standardized protocols.

section_path: Immunotherapeutic strategies targeting the gut microbiota
FMT
observations.text: FMT’s clinical translation faces challenges. Safety concerns include infectious complications (97) while donor variation complicates standardization, transplanted microbe stability remains uncertain, and regulatory ambiguity hampers multicenter randomized controlled trials (RCTs). Moving forward, personalized donor-recipient matching algorithms and non-invasive delivery systems such as lyophilized capsules could enhance clinical feasibility.

section_path: Immunotherapeutic strategies targeting the gut microbiota
FMT
observations.text: Consequently, the rational design of defined microbial consortia cultured under standardized conditions emerges as a prudent strategy to circumvent the safety concerns inherent in whole-microbiota transplantation. Continued efforts to refine donor selection criteria, optimize microbial preparation methods, and establish standardized safety monitoring protocols are essential to maximize therapeutic efficacy while minimizing infectious complications. These measures will ensure that FMT evolves as a safe and effective precision therapy in both infectious disease and oncology contexts.

section_path: Immunotherapeutic strategies targeting the gut microbiota
Probiotics
observations.text: Probiotics have emerged as a promising therapeutic modality in immunotherapy, with growing evidence supporting their role in enhancing tumor immunotherapy outcomes. As adjunctive agents in anticancer therapy, probiotics effectively modulate post-treatment immune dysregulation and alleviate treatment-related adverse effects, thereby potentiating the efficacy of both chemotherapy and immunotherapy regimens.

section_path: Immunotherapeutic strategies targeting the gut microbiota
Probiotics
observations.text: Griffin et al. revealed that live Enterococcus secretes SagA, a peptidoglycan hydrolase generating immunostimulatory fragments which enhance checkpoint inhibitor response (98). They subsequently engineered SagA-expressing probiotics and synthetic analogs, experimentally validating their ability to boost anti-PD-L1 efficacy. Moreover, Kawanabe-Matsuda et al. demonstrated that specific probiotic strains, notably Lactobacillus delbrueckii subsp. bulgaricus, potentiate ICI efficacy by expanding CCR6^{+} CD8^{+} T cell populations, thereby amplifying antitumor immunity (99).

section_path: Immunotherapeutic strategies targeting the gut microbiota
Probiotics
observations.text: Three emerging next-generation probiotics, including Bacteroides fragilis, Faecalibacterium prausnitzii, and Akkermansia, modulate gastrointestinal immunity through metabolite production, pathogen exclusion, and barrier reinforcement, with select B. fragilis isolates demonstrating particular promise for improving immunotherapy responsiveness (100,101). The growing body of evidence underscores the potential of probiotics as precision therapeutic agents in oncology, offering a multifaceted approach to improving treatment outcomes through microbiome modulation.

section_path: Immunotherapeutic strategies targeting the gut microbiota
Probiotics
observations.text: Compelling evidence from independent research highlights the therapeutic potential of butyrate-mediated immunomodulation by probiotics in cancer immunotherapy. Complementary findings reveal that the probiotic formulation LGG Probio-M9 enhances colonization of beneficial commensals including Lactobacillus and Bifidobacterium animalis. These symbionts generate butyrate and other immunomodulatory metabolites that concurrently promote CTL infiltration/activation and suppress Treg accumulation within tumors, substantially improving therapeutic outcomes (102). Faecalibacterium prausnitzii also potentiates anti-PD-L1 monoclonal antibody therapy by producing butyrate, which downregulates PD-L1 expression and augments cytotoxic CD8^{+} T cell levels in the TME (103).

section_path: Immunotherapeutic strategies targeting the gut microbiota
Probiotics
observations.text: Mechanistic studies in pancreatic cancer models elucidate LGG’s dual therapeutic action, which attenuates Toll-like receptor signaling in malignant cells, downregulating PD-L1 and interleukin-1β expression while reducing immunosuppressive myeloid cell infiltration. The resultant pro-inflammatory microenvironment facilitates CTL-mediated tumor clearance, establishing LGG as a multimodal adjuvant for pancreatic cancer immunotherapy (104). In the microsatellite stable CRC model, supplementation with Alistipes onderdonkii promoted intratumoral CD8^{+} T cell infiltration, inhibited the JAK/STAT pathway, and restored intestinal barrier integrity, providing a potential adjuvant strategy for overcoming immunotherapy resistance (105).

section_path: Immunotherapeutic strategies targeting the gut microbiota
Probiotics
observations.text: Nevertheless, contrasting evidence has emerged regarding probiotic interventions in cancer immunotherapy. Experimental models utilizing low-fiber dietary regimens or probiotic supplementation have demonstrated compromised anti-PD-1 therapeutic efficacy, characterized by significantly diminished IFN-γ^{+} CTL frequencies within the TME (106). Such research should aim to establish optimal therapeutic parameters while systematically evaluating both beneficial and potentially adverse outcomes associated with microbiota-targeted interventions in cancer immunotherapy.

section_path: Immunotherapeutic strategies targeting the gut microbiota
Engineered microbes
observations.text: The rapid evolution of genetic engineering technologies has catalyzed a global research revolution in engineered microbial therapeutics. Unlike natural microbial consortia, these precision-designed organisms possess disease-sensing capabilities and site-specific therapeutic responsiveness.

section_path: Immunotherapeutic strategies targeting the gut microbiota
Engineered microbes
observations.text: Rather than simple bacterial supplementation, these platforms actively reprogram the TME. Canale et al. engineered E. coli Nissle 1917 to colonize tumors and convert ammonia to L-arginine, directly altering metabolic competition (107). Redenti’s group advanced this chassis into a vaccine platform that enhances neo-epitope delivery and biosafety, eliciting robust tumor-specific T cell responses against primary and metastatic lesions (108). Similarly, Mycobacterium smegmatis engineered to secrete a PD-L1 inhibitor/IL-15 fusion protein activates cGAS-STING pathways while remodeling the TME, achieving systemic abscopal effects (109).

section_path: Immunotherapeutic strategies targeting the gut microbiota
Engineered microbes
observations.text: These metabolic and immune-activating platforms are complemented by bacteria that synergize directly with ICIs. Salmonella typhimurium combined with PD-L1 blockade drives tumor-specific CD8^{+} T cell expansion and complete regression (110), while Listeria monocytogenes vaccines paired with anti-PD-1 amplify peripheral CD8^{+} T cell infiltration and antigen-specific immunity, suggesting bacterial adjuvants can overcome resistance (111).

section_path: Immunotherapeutic strategies targeting the gut microbiota
Engineered microbes
observations.text: Advancing delivery precision, He et al. developed Bifidobacterium bifidum loaded with doxorubicin nanoparticles, synergizing local cytotoxicity with immunomodulation to suppress primary tumors and metastases (112). A parallel innovation employs controlled lysis-release probiotics for intratumoral deployment of PD-L1/CTLA-4 nanobodies, enhancing activated T cells while eliciting durable systemic immunity and memory expansion (113).

section_path: Immunotherapeutic strategies targeting the gut microbiota
Engineered microbes
observations.text: Together, these studies illustrate a critical evolution—from passive microbial modulation to active TME reprogramming. While metabolic engineering addresses nutrient competition, immune-activating platforms directly reshape immune landscapes. Delivery systems further refine specificity, yet challenges remain: optimizing tumor colonization, minimizing off-target toxicity, and validating long-term safety across cancer types will determine clinical translatability.

section_path: Immunotherapeutic strategies targeting the gut microbiota
Other therapeutic approaches
observations.text: Gram-negative bacteria naturally produce outer membrane vesicles (OMVs), nanoscale spherical structures composed of outer membrane proteins and immunologically active components. These OMVs have emerged as potent immunotherapeutic agents, demonstrating significant potential across multiple tumor immunotherapy paradigms (114-119). Concurrently, bacteriophage-based therapies represent a novel frontier in anticancer treatment, capable of simultaneously modulating gut microbiota composition, systemic immunity, and TME dynamics. A recent innovative approach combining dextran nanoparticle-encapsulated irinotecan with Fn-targeting bacteriophages demonstrated enhanced therapeutic efficacy in CRC models, highlighting the potential of phage-mediated precision immunotherapy (120).

section_path: Immunotherapeutic strategies targeting the gut microbiota
Other therapeutic approaches
observations.text: The field of microbiota-mediated tumor immunotherapy encompasses diverse and promising therapeutic strategies, ranging from engineered probiotics to bacteriophage interventions. However, significant knowledge gaps and technical challenges remain, necessitating continued mechanistic investigation and clinical validation. Sustained investment in this rapidly evolving field will be crucial for translating preclinical discoveries into clinically viable treatments, ultimately revolutionizing cancer therapeutic paradigms.

section_path: Immunotherapeutic strategies targeting the gut microbiota
Translational challenges and future directions
observations.text: From an evidence perspective, current support for microbiota-based interventions in cancer immunotherapy remains limited. Most available data are derived from retrospective cohort studies or small-phase clinical trials, and large-scale RCTs validating FMT or probiotics as adjuvants to ICIs are still lacking (121). From a translational standpoint, several key bottlenecks must be addressed, particularly with respect to safety and standardization. FMT carries risks of transmitting drug-resistant pathogens, while the colonization stability and reproducibility of probiotic interventions remain unpredictable (97). In addition, regulatory frameworks governing microbiota-based therapies are not yet fully established. Furthermore, pronounced inter-individual heterogeneity in baseline microbiome composition underscores the necessity of personalized therapeutic strategies (122). Looking ahead, future precision-oriented treatment paradigms should integrate microbiome profiling with host genetic characteristics to enable patient stratification, thereby facilitating a shift from one-size-fits-all approaches toward targeted microbial consortia or metabolite-based interventions.

section_path: Conclusions
observations.text: This review systematically synthesizes the mechanisms by which the gut microbiota-metabolite-immune axis modulates antitumor immunity across tumor types, confirming microbiota-targeted interventions as effective strategies to overcome ICI resistance. FMT, probiotics, and engineered microbes demonstrate translational potential for reshaping immune responses and enhancing therapeutic efficacy. Future studies employing multi-omics approaches to precisely identify immunostimulatory strains and optimize personalized intervention protocols will be pivotal for advancing precision immuno-oncology and facilitating the translation of mechanistic discoveries into clinical practice.

Background and Objective Microbiota and their metabolites form a dynamic regulatory network that modulates the tumor microenvironment (TME) and immune cell functionality, emerging as critical targets in cancer immunotherapy. Despite remarkable advances in immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICIs), clinical efficacy remains limited by primary or acquired resistance in a substantial proportion of patients. Accumulating evidence indicates that the gut microbiota-metabolite-immune axis is a critical determinant of ICI responsiveness, but the underlying molecular mechanisms and tumor-specific regulatory patterns remain incompletely elucidated. This narrative review aims to systematically dissect the mechanistic interplay of this axis across diverse cancer types and synthesize current microbiota-targeted therapeutic strategies for improved immunotherapy outcomes. Methods We conducted a systematic literature search of PubMed for studies published between January 2019 and December 2025, with a particular focus on basic and translational research elucidating the roles of gut microbiota and their metabolites in cancer immunotherapy across various malignancies. Key Content and Findings This review elucidates the molecular mechanisms by which core metabolites regulate antitumor immunity, synthesizes characteristic microbial signatures across gastrointestinal and non-gastrointestinal cancers. Furthermore, we evaluate the translational potential of intervention strategies, including fecal microbiota transplantation, probiotic supplementation, and engineered microbes, as adjuvants to enhance ICI efficacy and overcome resistance. Conclusions Microbiota-based personalized therapeutic strategies are increasingly recognized as promising tools to modulate antitumor immunity and improve immunotherapy outcomes. Systematic profiling of the gut microbiota-metabolite-immune axis across cancer types will facilitate the development of precision interventions to overcome ICI resistance. Future research integrating multi-omics approaches and large-scale clinical trials is pivotal to translate mechanistic insights into clinically viable therapies, ultimately revolutionizing the landscape of cancer immuno-oncology.

Inosine is a critical intermediary in the purine nucleotide metabolic pathway and is synthesized by gut microbiota such as Bifidobacterium pseudolongum, Lactobacillus johnsonii, and bacteria of the genus Olsenella (24). This microbial-derived metabolite plays essential roles in posttranscriptional gene regulation, modulation of metabolic enzyme activities, and integration into cellular signaling networks (25). Notably, immune checkpoint blockade (ICB) therapy impairs gut barrier integrity, facilitating the translocation of inosine into the systemic circulation and subsequent activation of antitumor T cells, establishing inosine as the key molecule mediating the enhancement of ICB efficacy by these bacteria (24). Currently, inosine exerts three principal effects in antitumor therapy. Firstly, it markedly enhances tumor immunogenicity. Zhang et al. employed advanced metabolomic profiling to analyze plasma samples from melanoma-bearing mice undergoing ICI treatment, revealing a novel mechanism: inosine specifically inhibits ubiquitin-like modifier-activating enzyme 6 (UBA6) activity within tumor cells, leading to a marked increase in tumor immunogenicity (52). This dual-purpose finding identifies UBA6 as a therapeutic target and rationalizes inosine-based combination therapy. Secondly, inosine plays distinct roles in immune cell modulation and metabolic support. Microbial-derived inosine binds to adenosine A2A receptors on T lymphocytes, triggering activation of the cAMP-CREB signaling cascade. This pathway facilitates the differentiation and tumor infiltration of T helper 1 (Th1) cells within the tumor microenvironment (TME), amplifying antitumor immune responses (24). Thirdly, and most critically, inosine functions as a compensatory metabolic substrate that sustains T cell bioenergetics under glucose-restricted TME conditions. Wang et al. experimentally demonstrated that effector T cells utilize inosine as an alternative energy source during glucose deprivation, sustaining their survival, proliferation, and cytotoxic functions (53). Clinically, this dual functionality holds therapeutic promise.

observations.text: The human body hosts a vast and complex microbial ecosystem, comprising approximately 40 trillion microorganisms comprising around 3,000 distinct microbial species (1). The human gastrointestinal microbial community represents a highly intricate ecosystem, with the colon serving as the primary habitat for bacterial colonization and playing a decisive role in shaping the total bacterial load within the human body (2). section_path: Introduction

observations.text: A growing body of research has elucidated that gut microbiota plays a crucial role in the therapeutic efficacy of immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICIs) (5-9). In recent years, immunotherapy has emerged as a prominent therapeutic approach in the management of malignant tumors. The earliest identified ICIs primarily consisted of three categories: anti-programmed cell death protein 1 (PD-1), anti-programmed death-ligand 1 (PD-L1), and anti-cytotoxic T-lymphocyte-associated antigen-4 (CTLA-4) monoclonal antibodies. Recent discoveries of novel immune checkpoints have not only expanded the repertoire of therapeutic targets but also provided new perspectives for personalized cancer treatment. Noteworthy examples are lymphocyte-activation gene-3 (LAG-3), T-cell immunoglobulin and mucin-domain-containing 3 (TIM-3), T-cell immunoglobulin and ITIM domain (TIGIT), and V-domain Ig suppressor of T-cell activation (VISTA), among others (10).

observations.text: However, a notable proportion of patients who initially respond to ICI therapy ultimately develop acquired resistance (11), representing a major clinical challenge. Therefore, current advancements in gastrointestinal microbiome research represent a meaningful and novel direction for addressing immunotherapy resistance in oncology. However, the underlying molecular mechanisms through which gut microbiota and their metabolites influence immunotherapy efficacy remain poorly understood across cancer types. This review systematically examines microbiota-metabolite interactions affecting ICI outcomes and explores therapeutic implications. observations.text: The core of the gut microbiota-metabolite-immune axis lies in the production of diverse bioactive metabolites by the gut microbiota through its metabolic activities. These metabolites act as molecular messengers within the axis, not only regulating host energy metabolism and nutrient absorption but, more crucially, reprogramming antitumor immune responses (11). Notably, the dynamic nature of this axis is reflected in the ability of these metabolites to translocate from the intestinal lumen into systemic circulation, exerting pleiotropic effects on both local and systemic antitumor immunity, thereby modulating therapeutic responses to ICIs across multiple cancer types (6,12,13). Figure 1 and Table 2 systematically illustrate the key node networks of metabolite-immune interactions within this axis, revealing its translational potential as a druggable target.

observations.text: The integrated mechanisms by which gut microbial metabolites shape antitumor immunity by steering the fate of immune cells. Butyrate, the best-studied SCFA, exerts multifaceted and context-dependent effects: it inhibits HDAC activity to activate M2-like tumor-associated macrophages in lung cancer, yet concurrently enhances the cytotoxic capacity of CD8^{+} T cells, boosts ROS production, and thereby suppresses tumor-cell proliferation and metastasis. Tryptophan catabolites activate the AhR via the IDO1-Kyn axis, expanding Tregs and fostering an immunosuppressive niche. Among secondary BAs, UDCA degrades TGF-β and consequently restrains Treg differentiation, whereas isoDCA impairs dendritic-cell function and indirectly promotes Treg accumulation. Inosine engages the A2AR to raise intracellular cAMP, tipping the balance toward Th1-cell differentiation. The net outcome of these opposing metabolic signals determines whether the tumor micro-environment remains cold or becomes hot. Collectively, the scheme underscores that the tripartite interplay among microbial metabolites, host receptors, and immune cells constitutes a central rheostat of cancer immunosurveillance. observations.text: The gut microbiota, as a highly complex ecosystem, produces a diverse array of bioactive metabolites through metabolic activities, which serve as the initial signals of the gut microbiota-metabolite-immune axis. Functioning as the key signaling branch of this axis, these metabolites systematically regulate both innate and adaptive immunity through mechanisms such as receptor engagement, epigenetic remodeling, and metabolic reprogramming. This dynamic regulatory network demonstrates that distinct microbial communities can exert differential effects on the immune system via their specific metabolic products. The following sections will focus on various core metabolites, elaborating on their source microorganisms, characteristic functions, and the immune regulatory mechanisms they mediate.

observations.text: SCFAs are produced as metabolic by-products during the fermentation of complex carbohydrates and dietary fiber. This bioconversion is predominantly driven by bacterial species within the Bacteroidetes phylum, particularly those belonging to the genera Bacteroides, Prevotella, Parabacteroides, and Alistipes. Their high expression of carbohydrate-active enzymes confers a robust degradative capacity, enabling efficient substrate utilization (26-28).

observations.text: Butyrate exhibits antitumor properties through multiple, context-dependent pathways. A key mechanism involves histone deacetylase (HDAC) inhibition. It suppresses HDAC activity, butyrate increases protein acetylation, thereby downregulating NFATc3 and inhibiting tumor cell proliferation (29) yet paradoxically promotes lung cancer metastasis by suppressing HDAC2, drives M2 macrophage polarization and upregulates H19 expression in tumor cells (30). Faecalibaculum rodentium-derived metabolites propionate and butyrate enhance histone acetylation to promote progenitor-exhausted CD8^{+} T cells expansion, thereby activating antitumor immune responses (31).

observations.text: G-protein-coupled receptor 109A (GPR109A) and reactive oxygen species (ROS) may represent critical pathways through which butyrate regulates tumor proliferation and therapeutic efficacy. Beyond epigenetic modulation, butyrate enhances CD8^{+} T cell cytotoxicity via the GPR109A/HOPX signaling axis, offering therapeutic potential in gastric cancer (GC) (14), and induces apoptosis in colonic epithelial cells through GPR109A binding (32). In hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC), butyrate supplementation activates calcium signaling and ROS generation, disrupting intracellular calcium homeostasis and attenuating tumor growth and metastasis (33). Additionally, butyrate modulates miR-22 expression in hepatocytes, promoting apoptosis via ROS accumulation, cytochrome C release, and caspase-3 activation (34).

observations.text: Subsequent mechanistic studies have delineated that butyrate enhances anti-PD-1 efficacy by activating CD8^{+} T cells through multiple, complementary routes. It intensifies T-cell receptor (TCR) signaling (15) and engages Toll-like receptor 5 (TLR5), triggering NF-κB-dependent transcriptional programs (6) that expand and energize the cytotoxic T-cell pool (35,36). These findings highlight the considerable potential of butyrate to serve as a therapeutic biomarker that modulates CD8^{+} T-cell-mediated antitumor immunity.

observations.text: Butyrate exerts bidirectional, context-dependent immunomodulatory effects by remodeling dendritic cell (DC) function. Its core mechanism involves inhibiting DC maturation markers—blocking CD80/CD86 upregulation and preventing pro-T helper 17 (Th17) polarization—to differentially regulate T cell responses. In anti-CTLA-4 therapy, this reduces DC-mediated T cell activation, impairing intratumoral infiltration of inducible T-cell co-stimulator (ICOS)^{+} tumor-specific T cells and memory T cells, thus weakening efficacy (16). Conversely, in myeloma, butyrate-producing Prevotella melaninogenica suppresses the DC-Th17 axis to reduce Th17 accumulation, promotes effector CD8^{+} T cell differentiation, and synergizes with anti-PD-L1 for antitumor effects (37). The paradoxical observations outlined above reveal that SCFA-mediated immune regulation is profoundly context-dependent, with functional outcomes dictated by tumor-specific immune infiltration landscapes and host metabolic states. This mechanistic complexity necessitates that future studies transcend reductive dichotomies, instead establishing predictive models grounded in integrated multi-omics analyses.

observations.text: Propionate and valerate also contribute to tumor immunotherapy. Notably, propionate produced by Akkermansia muciniphila (Akk) induces tumor cell apoptosis through mechanisms involving mitochondrial dysfunction and caspase activation (38). Both valerate and butyrate modulate mechanistic target of rapamycin (mTOR) signaling, a central regulator of cellular metabolism, while concurrently inhibiting class I HDAC activity. This dual mechanism facilitates metabolic and epigenetic reprogramming, resulting in upregulated expression of effector molecules such as CD25, interferon-γ (IFN-γ), and tumor necrosis factor-alpha (TNF-α). observations.text: The therapeutic efficacy of immunotherapy is intrinsically linked to the tumor immune microenvironment (TIME), wherein intratumoral microbial communities emerge as critical modulators. These microbial populations influence patient responses to ICIs through dynamic remodeling of the TIME. Streptococcus enrichment in responders correlates with enhanced CD8^{+} T-cell infiltration (62) while Fusobacterium nucleatum (Fn) drives resistance through PD-L1 upregulation and T cell suppression (63,64). Dual immunosuppressive pathways significantly impair local antitumor immunity, resulting in markedly reduced ICI responsiveness among patients with esophageal squamous cell carcinoma (ESCC) (64). Moreover, a prospective study has simultaneously revealed that low gut α-diversity also predicts poor response and shorter survival in the same cancer type (65). Consequently, the ESCC microenvironment should be viewed as an integrated ecosystem in which the collective action of the entire gut microbial community, rather than a single pathobiont, dictates therapeutic outcomes. Liang’s team systematically analyzed the gut microbial composition of 68 patients with ESCC and established a predictive model with high accuracy of neoadjuvant immunochemotherapy (NICT) response in ESCC using machine learning-based baseline gut bacterial strain signatures (66). Enabling precision medicine approaches for patient stratification and therapeutic target identification holds significant promise for future clinical translation.

observations.text: GC arises from multifactorial etiopathogenesis, with intratumoral microbial communities emerging as critical modulators of disease progression. Among these, Helicobacter pylori (H. pylori) occupies a central role in gastric carcinogenesis, employing both direct virulence factor-mediated mechanisms and indirect microbiome-modulating strategies (67). H. pylori effectively subverts antitumor immunity by creating an immune-protective niche for malignant cells while upregulating PD-L1 expression in gastric epithelium—a key immune evasion mechanism that inhibits cytotoxic T-cell-mediated tumor clearance (68).

observations.text: While H. pylori continues to dominate diagnostic and therapeutic pipelines, large-scale microbiome surveys of GC patients from two demographically distinct cohorts now reveal significant enrichments of Lactobacillus, Streptococcus, Prevotella and Bacteroides within tumor tissue (69). These data underscore that the GC microbiome extends well beyond H. pylori, warranting comprehensive investigation of multi-species microbial networks that collectively influence disease progression and therapeutic response. H. pylori upregulates PD-L1 to subvert immunity, but a study also found that Lactobacillus abundance correlates with enhanced microbial α-diversity, superior anti-PD-1/PD-L1 response rates and a favorable progression-free survival trend (70). These convergent findings identify H. pylori and Lactobacillus as a keystone taxon whose enrichment predicts enhanced ICI responsiveness while preserving microbiome homeostasis.

observations.text: PDAC is the most common malignant pancreatic tumor and the third leading cause of cancer-related death worldwide. Studies have indicated that three bacterial species, namely Elizabethkingia, Enterobacteriaceae, and Mycoplasmataceae play a role in influencing both the progression of PDAC and the response to PD-1 treatment (72). This phenotypic shift correlates mechanistically with enhanced CD4^{+} and CD8^{+} T-cell activation within the TME.

observations.text: HCC is a highly aggressive malignancy with dismal prognostic outcomes. It ranks among the leading causes of global cancer-related mortality, thereby imposing a substantial burden on public health (76). Recent clinical trials have shown that ICIs targeting PD-1 have demonstrated promising efficacy in the treatment of HCC (77,78). Building on these therapeutic advancements, emerging research has elucidated the crucial associations between the composition of the gut microbiota and the clinical efficacy of PD-1 immunotherapy in hepatobiliary malignancies. Mechanistic investigations have identified Akk and specific Ruminococcaceae species as microbial signatures correlated with enhanced therapeutic responses (12). Moreover, multi-center prospective cohorts, leveraging paired fecal metagenomics and metabolomics, have convergently identified a cluster of HCC-immunotherapy-favorable taxa—Lachnospiraceae-GAM79, Alistipes sp. Marseille-P5997, Ruminococcus, Erysipelotrichaceae-GAM147 (79), Lachnoclostridium and Lachnospiraceae (80)—enriched in responders, whereas Veillonellaceae (79) and Prevotella 9 (80) dominate in progressors. Parallel metabolic profiling of these signatures has mapped their functional output, laying a solid foundation for mechanistic dissection and therapeutic exploitation. Emerging evidence reveals that gut microbiota modulates CRC antitumor immunity through multifaceted mechanisms. Studies demonstrated that Lactobacillus rhamnosus GG (LGG) (8) and Fn (85) both upregulates activates the cGAS/STING axis to enhance anti-tumor immunity. LGG activates the cGAS/STING axis in CRC and melanoma models, which in turn stimulates type I interferon production in DCs (8). observations.text: Current research has revealed that microbiota can infiltrate tumor tissues through three primary pathways to influence tumor progression and therapeutic outcomes: direct mucosal invasion, penetration into adjacent normal tissues (NAT), and systemic dissemination via the circulatory system (87). This phenomenon extends beyond gastrointestinal malignancies, indicating that gut microbiota significantly contributes to the pathogenesis of non-digestive tract tumors. In 2015, two landmark studies published in Science, first elucidated the mechanistic role of gut microbiota in modulating immunotherapy responses in melanoma, establishing a critical foundation for this field. These two studies first elucidated the underlying mechanisms by which Commensal Bifidobacterium, B. thetaiotaomicron, and B. fragilis in the gut microbiota mediate the responses to melanoma immunotherapy (5,88). Subsequent investigations have systematically compared responders and non-responders to immunotherapy through comprehensive analyses of gut microbiome diversity and compositional variations, complemented by animal experimentation. These studies consistently demonstrate that patients with favorable gut microbial profiles exhibit enhanced systemic immunity and anti-tumor responses. Notably, FMT experiments have confirmed that germ-free mice receiving transplants from responder patients acquire improved immunocompetence and tumor control capabilities (89-91).

FMT

observations.text: FMT is a therapeutic intervention involving the transfer of donor gut microbiota, which has been established as a primary strategy for whole-microbiome reconstitution and is formally recommended in clinical guidelines for recurrent Clostridioides difficile infection (rCDI). FMT has emerged as a promising therapeutic modality for diverse conditions, including inflammatory bowel disease (IBD), metabolic syndrome, and solid malignancies. Despite decades of clinical reliance on combined chemotherapy and immunotherapy regimens, the limited efficacy of ICIs as monotherapy has driven exploration of microbiome-based therapeutic adjuvants. Seminal work in 2018 demonstrated that transferring fecal microbiota from ICI-responsive patients into germ-free or antibiotic-pretreated murine models enhanced ICI antitumor efficacy, establishing a causal link between gut microbiota composition and therapeutic outcomes (94). Subsequent studies have further validated this approach. Derosa et al. observed that fecal transplants from ICI-refractory RCC patients conferred reduced treatment responsiveness in RCC-bearing mice, while Wang et al. reported that transferring microbiota from microsatellite-stable colorectal cancer (MSS-CRC) patients with high Fn burdens into germ-free MSS-CRC models increased sensitivity to anti-PD-1 therapy (9).

observations.text: Clinical studies confirm FMT’s potential to enhance ICI efficacy. Baruch et al. reported two partial and one complete response in refractory melanoma patients receiving FMT plus anti-PD-1, demonstrating the feasibility of FMT as an adjunct to immunotherapy (95). Building on these findings, Routy et al. performed a multicenter phase I trial in 20 treatment-naïve patients with advanced melanoma, combining healthy donor FMT with PD-1 inhibitors (nivolumab or pembrolizumab). The trial reported an objective response rate of 65%, including four complete responses, while concurrently establishing the safety profile of FMT in this therapeutic context (96). Recent metagenomic analyses further identified favorable mycobiome enterotypes that enrich butyrate-producing bacteria and enhance CD8^{+} T cell infiltration when selected as donors (36). Based on this study, clinicians could optimize therapeutic precision. This multi-kingdom approach represents a paradigm shift from traditional bacteria-centric donor screening, potentially improving patient outcomes in cancer immunotherapy. Prospective validation across diverse malignancies will be essential to establish standardized protocols.
