Safety concerns include infectious complications (97) while donor variation complicates standardization, transplanted microbe stability remains uncertain, and regulatory ambiguity hampers multicenter randomized controlled trials (RCTs). Moving forward, personalized donor-recipient matching algorithms and non-invasive delivery systems such as lyophilized capsules could enhance clinical feasibility.

observations.text: Probiotics have emerged as a promising therapeutic modality in immunotherapy, with growing evidence supporting their role in enhancing tumor immunotherapy outcomes. As adjunctive agents in anticancer therapy, probiotics effectively modulate post-treatment immune dysregulation and alleviate treatment-related adverse effects, thereby potentiating the efficacy of both chemotherapy and immunotherapy regimens.

observations.text: Griffin et al. revealed that live Enterococcus secretes SagA, a peptidoglycan hydrolase generating immunostimulatory fragments which enhance checkpoint inhibitor response (98). They subsequently engineered SagA-expressing probiotics and synthetic analogs, experimentally validating their ability to boost anti-PD-L1 efficacy. Moreover, Kawanabe-Matsuda et al. demonstrated that specific probiotic strains, notably Lactobacillus delbrueckii subsp. bulgaricus, potentiate ICI efficacy by expanding CCR6^{+} CD8^{+} T cell populations, thereby amplifying antitumor immunity (99).

observations.text: Three emerging next-generation probiotics, including Bacteroides fragilis, Faecalibacterium prausnitzii, and Akkermansia, modulate gastrointestinal immunity through metabolite production, pathogen exclusion, and barrier reinforcement, with select B. fragilis isolates demonstrating particular promise for improving immunotherapy responsiveness (100,101). The growing body of evidence underscores the potential of probiotics as precision therapeutic agents in oncology, offering a multifaceted approach to improving treatment outcomes through microbiome modulation.

observations.text: Compelling evidence from independent research highlights the therapeutic potential of butyrate-mediated immunomodulation by probiotics in cancer immunotherapy. Complementary findings reveal that the probiotic formulation LGG Probio-M9 enhances colonization of beneficial commensals including Lactobacillus and Bifidobacterium animalis. These symbionts generate butyrate and other immunomodulatory metabolites that concurrently promote CTL infiltration/activation and suppress Treg accumulation within tumors, substantially improving therapeutic outcomes (102). Faecalibacterium prausnitzii also potentiates anti-PD-L1 monoclonal antibody therapy by producing butyrate, which downregulates PD-L1 expression and augments cytotoxic CD8^{+} T cell levels in the TME (103).

observations.text: Mechanistic studies in pancreatic cancer models elucidate LGG’s dual therapeutic action, which attenuates Toll-like receptor signaling in malignant cells, downregulating PD-L1 and interleukin-1β expression while reducing immunosuppressive myeloid cell infiltration. The resultant pro-inflammatory microenvironment facilitates CTL-mediated tumor clearance, establishing LGG as a multimodal adjuvant for pancreatic cancer immunotherapy (104). In the microsatellite stable CRC model, supplementation with Alistipes onderdonkii promoted intratumoral CD8^{+} T cell infiltration, inhibited the JAK/STAT pathway, and restored intestinal barrier integrity, providing a potential adjuvant strategy for overcoming immunotherapy resistance (105).

Experimental models utilizing low-fiber dietary regimens or probiotic supplementation have demonstrated compromised anti-PD-1 therapeutic efficacy, characterized by significantly diminished IFN-γ^{+} CTL frequencies within the TME (106). Such research should aim to establish optimal therapeutic parameters while systematically evaluating both beneficial and potentially adverse outcomes associated with microbiota-targeted interventions in cancer immunotherapy.

Unlike natural microbial consortia, these precision-designed organisms possess disease-sensing capabilities and site-specific therapeutic responsiveness.

Canale et al. engineered E. coli Nissle 1917 to colonize tumors and convert ammonia to L-arginine, directly altering metabolic competition (107). Redenti’s group advanced this chassis into a vaccine platform that enhances neo-epitope delivery and biosafety, eliciting robust tumor-specific T cell responses against primary and metastatic lesions (108). Similarly, Mycobacterium smegmatis engineered to secrete a PD-L1 inhibitor/IL-15 fusion protein activates cGAS-STING pathways while remodeling the TME, achieving systemic abscopal effects (109).

A parallel innovation employs controlled lysis-release probiotics for intratumoral deployment of PD-L1/CTLA-4 nanobodies, enhancing activated T cells while eliciting durable systemic immunity and memory expansion (113).

While metabolic engineering addresses nutrient competition, immune-activating platforms directly reshape immune landscapes. Delivery systems further refine specificity, yet challenges remain: optimizing tumor colonization, minimizing off-target toxicity, and validating long-term safety across cancer types will determine clinical translatability.

observations.text: Gram-negative bacteria naturally produce outer membrane vesicles (OMVs), nanoscale spherical structures composed of outer membrane proteins and immunologically active components. These OMVs have emerged as potent immunotherapeutic agents, demonstrating significant potential across multiple tumor immunotherapy paradigms (114-119). Concurrently, bacteriophage-based therapies represent a novel frontier in anticancer treatment, capable of simultaneously modulating gut microbiota composition, systemic immunity, and TME dynamics. A recent innovative approach combining dextran nanoparticle-encapsulated irinotecan with Fn-targeting bacteriophages demonstrated enhanced therapeutic efficacy in CRC models, highlighting the potential of phage-mediated precision immunotherapy (120).

observations.text: The field of microbiota-mediated tumor immunotherapy encompasses diverse and promising therapeutic strategies, ranging from engineered probiotics to bacteriophage interventions. However, significant knowledge gaps and technical challenges remain, necessitating continued mechanistic investigation and clinical validation. Sustained investment in this rapidly evolving field will be crucial for translating preclinical discoveries into clinically viable treatments, ultimately revolutionizing cancer therapeutic paradigms.

Translational challenges and future directions

observations.text: From an evidence perspective, current support for microbiota-based interventions in cancer immunotherapy remains limited. Most available data are derived from retrospective cohort studies or small-phase clinical trials, and large-scale RCTs validating FMT or probiotics as adjuvants to ICIs are still lacking (121). From a translational standpoint, several key bottlenecks must be addressed, particularly with respect to safety and standardization. FMT carries risks of transmitting drug-resistant pathogens, while the colonization stability and reproducibility of probiotic interventions remain unpredictable (97). In addition, regulatory frameworks governing microbiota-based therapies are not yet fully established. Furthermore, pronounced inter-individual heterogeneity in baseline microbiome composition underscores the necessity of personalized therapeutic strategies (122). Looking ahead, future precision-oriented treatment paradigms should integrate microbiome profiling with host genetic characteristics to enable patient stratification, thereby facilitating a shift from one-size-fits-all approaches toward targeted microbial consortia or metabolite-based interventions.

observations.text: This review systematically synthesizes the mechanisms by which the gut microbiota-metabolite-immune axis modulates antitumor immunity across tumor types, confirming microbiota-targeted interventions as effective strategies to overcome ICI resistance. FMT, probiotics, and engineered microbes demonstrate translational potential for reshaping immune responses and enhancing therapeutic efficacy. Future studies employing multi-omics approaches to precisely identify immunostimulatory strains and optimize personalized intervention protocols will be pivotal for advancing precision immuno-oncology and facilitating the translation of mechanistic discoveries into clinical practice.

observations.text: Background and Objective Microbiota and their metabolites form a dynamic regulatory network that modulates the tumor microenvironment (TME) and immune cell functionality, emerging as critical targets in cancer immunotherapy. Despite remarkable advances in immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICIs), clinical efficacy remains limited by primary or acquired resistance in a substantial proportion of patients. Accumulating evidence indicates that the gut microbiota-metabolite-immune axis is a critical determinant of ICI responsiveness, but the underlying molecular mechanisms and tumor-specific regulatory patterns remain incompletely elucidated. This narrative review aims to systematically dissect the mechanistic interplay of this axis across diverse cancer types and synthesize current microbiota-targeted therapeutic strategies for improved immunotherapy outcomes. Methods We conducted a systematic literature search of PubMed for studies published between January 2019 and December 2025, with a particular focus on basic and translational research elucidating the roles of gut microbiota and their metabolites in cancer immunotherapy across various malignancies. Key Content and Findings This review elucidates the molecular mechanisms by which core metabolites regulate antitumor immunity, synthesizes characteristic microbial signatures across gastrointestinal and non-gastrointestinal cancers. Furthermore, we evaluate the translational potential of intervention strategies, including fecal microbiota transplantation, probiotic supplementation, and engineered microbes, as adjuvants to enhance ICI efficacy and overcome resistance. Conclusions Microbiota-based personalized therapeutic strategies are increasingly recognized as promising tools to modulate antitumor immunity and improve immunotherapy outcomes. Systematic profiling of the gut microbiota-metabolite-immune axis across cancer types will facilitate the development of precision interventions to overcome ICI resistance. Future research integrating multi-omics approaches and large-scale clinical trials is pivotal to translate mechanistic insights into clinically viable therapies, ultimately revolutionizing the landscape of cancer immuno-oncology.

paper_identity.title: Targeting the gut microbiota-metabolite-immune axis in cancer immunotherapy: mechanistic interplay, therapeutic strategies, and translational applications-a narrative review

observations.text: Inosine is a critical intermediary in the purine nucleotide metabolic pathway and is synthesized by gut microbiota such as Bifidobacterium pseudolongum, Lactobacillus johnsonii, and bacteria of the genus Olsenella (24). This microbial-derived metabolite plays essential roles in posttranscriptional gene regulation, modulation of metabolic enzyme activities, and integration into cellular signaling networks (25). Notably, immune checkpoint blockade (ICB) therapy impairs gut barrier integrity, facilitating the translocation of inosine into the systemic circulation and subsequent activation of antitumor T cells, establishing inosine as the key molecule mediating the enhancement of ICB efficacy by these bacteria (24). Currently, inosine exerts three principal effects in antitumor therapy. Firstly, it markedly enhances tumor immunogenicity. Zhang et al. employed advanced metabolomic profiling to analyze plasma samples from melanoma-bearing mice undergoing ICI treatment, revealing a novel mechanism: inosine specifically inhibits ubiquitin-like modifier-activating enzyme 6 (UBA6) activity within tumor cells, leading to a marked increase in tumor immunogenicity (52). This dual-purpose finding identifies UBA6 as a therapeutic target and rationalizes inosine-based combination therapy. Secondly, inosine plays distinct roles in immune cell modulation and metabolic support. Microbial-derived inosine binds to adenosine A2A receptors on T lymphocytes, triggering activation of the cAMP-CREB signaling cascade. This pathway facilitates the differentiation and tumor infiltration of T helper 1 (Th1) cells within the tumor microenvironment (TME), amplifying antitumor immune responses (24). Thirdly, and most critically, inosine functions as a compensatory metabolic substrate that sustains T cell bioenergetics under glucose-restricted TME conditions. Wang et al. experimentally demonstrated that effector T cells utilize inosine as an alternative energy source during glucose deprivation, sustaining their survival, proliferation, and cytotoxic functions (53). Clinically, this dual functionality holds therapeutic promise.
